source: heart-knowledge-hub (curated primary sources) plus standard cardiac physiology

items.name: Heart
items.description: A four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a closed fist, sitting in the middle of the chest and tilted so its pointed end aims down and to the left. It runs two pumps back to back: one to the lungs, one to the rest of the body.
items.funFact: Over an average life it beats close to three billion times without a scheduled rest.

items.name: Mediastinum
items.description: The central compartment of the chest between the two lungs. It holds the heart, the great vessels, the thymus, part of the oesophagus and the trachea.
items.funFact: It is a shifting space: the heart moves within it every time you breathe.

items.name: Pericardium
items.description: A tough double-layered sac that wraps the heart and anchors it to the diaphragm and surrounding structures. The inner surface glides against the outer one.
items.funFact: The sac is only millimetres thick but strong enough to keep the heart from ballooning.

items.name: Pericardial fluid
items.description: A thin film of fluid between the two serous layers. It lubricates the surfaces so the heart can contract and twist with almost no friction.
items.funFact: Too much of it (a effusion) can squeeze the heart, because the fibrous sac will not stretch quickly.

items.name: Epicardium
items.description: The outermost layer of the heart wall, a thin sheet that is also the inner layer of the serous pericardium. Coronary vessels run inside it, cushioned by fat.
items.funFact: The fat you see on a heart surface sits in the epicardium, following the grooves between chambers.

items.name: Epicardial fat
items.description: Yellowish fat deposited along the coronary grooves and around the great vessels. It insulates, cushions and supplies fatty acids to the muscle beneath.
items.funFact: It is not inert padding: it releases signalling molecules that influence the heart's rhythm.

items.name: Myocardium
items.description: The working muscle of the heart, built from spiralling bundles of cardiomyocytes. Its fibres wrap the chambers in opposing helices so contraction both shortens and twists.
items.funFact: The helical fibre arrangement is why the heart wrings itself out like a wet towel rather than just crushing inward.

items.name: Endocardium
items.description: The smooth inner lining of the chambers and valves. It is continuous with the endothelium of the vessels, giving blood one uninterrupted non-stick surface.
items.funFact: A single cell layer thick in places, it must survive a lifetime of turbulent flow.

items.name: Apex
items.description: The pointed lower tip of the left ventricle, resting on the diaphragm. It is the spot where the heartbeat is easiest to feel.
items.funFact: Clinicians find it by touch: the apex beat is the left ventricle striking the chest wall.

items.name: Right atrium
items.description: The collecting chamber for oxygen-poor blood returning from the body through the two venae cavae. It passes blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
items.funFact: It also holds the heart's own pacemaker, a patch of cells that fires without being told to.

items.name: Right atrial appendage
items.description: A small ear-shaped pouch projecting from the right atrium. It adds volume when the atrium fills and contains pectinate muscle ridges.
items.funFact: Appendages are where clots most often form in atrial fibrillation, because blood can pool inside them.

items.name: Right ventricle
items.description: A crescent-shaped, thin-walled pump that pushes blood into the lungs at low pressure. It wraps partly around the thicker left ventricle.
items.funFact: It only needs a fifth of the left ventricle's pressure because the lungs are close and delicate.

items.name: Left atrium
items.description: The chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the four pulmonary veins and delivers it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.
items.funFact: It sits at the very back of the heart, which is why it is the chamber closest to the oesophagus.

items.name: Left atrial appendage
items.description: A narrow hooked pouch on the left atrium. In atrial fibrillation it can hold stagnant blood and is a common source of stroke-causing clots.
items.funFact: Devices can be implanted to seal it off, so clots cannot escape even if the rhythm stays irregular.

items.name: Left ventricle
items.description: The thickest, strongest chamber. It drives blood into the aorta against systemic pressure, forming the pointed apex of the heart.
items.funFact: Its muscle is roughly three times thicker than the right ventricle's, because the whole body is downstream.

items.name: Interatrial septum
items.description: The wall separating the two atria. In the fetus it carries a flap valve that lets blood bypass the lungs.
items.funFact: About one in four adults keeps a small probe-patent opening here, usually harmless.

items.name: Interventricular septum
items.description: The thick muscular wall between the ventricles. The upper part is thin and membranous; the lower part is muscle and contracts with the left ventricle.
items.funFact: A hole here (VSD) is the most common congenital heart defect, and small ones often close on their own.

items.name: Fossa ovalis
items.description: A shallow oval depression on the right side of the atrial septum. It is the sealed remnant of the fetal opening that once shunted blood past the lungs.
items.funFact: It is a fossil of your own circulation: a hole you needed before you could breathe air.

items.name: Trabeculae carneae
items.description: Rounded muscular ridges on the inside of the ventricles. They break up flow, add surface area and anchor the papillary muscles.
items.funFact: Their chaotic ridges are thought to smooth blood movement rather than disturb it.

items.name: Pectinate muscles
items.description: Comb-like ridges of muscle inside the atrial appendages. They let the thin atrial wall contract without folding on itself.
items.funFact: They look like the teeth of a comb, which is exactly what their Latin name means.

items.name: Moderator band
items.description: A muscular bridge across the right ventricular cavity that carries part of the conduction system to the free wall. It stops the thin wall overstretching.
items.funFact: It is a reliable landmark when you are looking at a scan and need to know which ventricle you are in.

items.name: Tricuspid valve
items.description: The three-leaflet inlet valve between the right atrium and right ventricle. It opens in diastole and shuts at the start of contraction.
items.funFact: It is the valve most often damaged by intravenous drug use and infection.

items.name: Pulmonary valve
items.description: A three-cusped valve at the exit of the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk. It opens only during ejection.
items.funFact: It has the lowest pressure load of all four valves, so it is rarely narrowed by wear alone.

items.name: Mitral valve
items.description: The two-leaflet valve between the left atrium and left ventricle. Its leaflets are tethered by cords so they cannot blow back into the atrium under high pressure.
items.funFact: It is the only valve with two leaflets, and the only one named after a bishop's hat.

items.name: Aortic valve
items.description: A three-cusped valve between the left ventricle and the aorta. Just above its cusps sit the openings of the coronary arteries.
items.funFact: The coronaries are fed by pockets behind the cusps, so the heart feeds itself at the moment it relaxes.

items.name: Chordae tendineae
items.description: Tough string-like cords linking the valve leaflets to the papillary muscles. They hold the leaflets shut against systolic pressure.
items.funFact: They are sometimes called the heartstrings, and they are under real tension every beat.

items.name: Papillary muscles
items.description: Finger-like muscles inside the ventricles that tighten during systole to keep the chordae taut, so the inlet valves cannot invert.
items.funFact: They do not open or close the valve; they only stop it from turning inside out.

items.name: Fibrous skeleton
items.description: A dense ring of connective tissue surrounding all four valves. It anchors them, electrically separates atria from ventricles and gives the muscle something to pull against.
facts: Only route between atria and ventricles is the AV node
items.funFact: Because it does not conduct electricity, the heart has exactly one electrical gateway between its upper and lower chambers.

items.name: Superior vena cava
items.description: The large vein bringing oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck and arms down into the right atrium.
items.funFact: It is thin-walled enough to collapse if pressure around the heart rises sharply.

items.name: Inferior vena cava
items.description: The largest vein in the body, returning blood from the abdomen, pelvis and legs to the right atrium. It passes through the diaphragm.
items.funFact: It carries the drug absorbed from the gut after it has already passed through the liver.

items.name: Pulmonary trunk
items.description: A short wide vessel leaving the right ventricle that splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries. It is the only artery in the body carrying oxygen-poor blood.
items.funFact: Arteries are defined by direction, not oxygen: this one carries blood away from the heart and still looks blue.

items.name: Pulmonary arteries
items.description: Branches that carry blood to each lung and divide repeatedly alongside the airways until they become capillaries around the alveoli.
items.funFact: The lungs are the only organ that receives the entire cardiac output.

items.name: Pulmonary veins
items.description: Four veins, two from each lung, delivering oxygen-rich blood into the left atrium. They are the only veins carrying bright red blood.
items.funFact: They are a common origin of the electrical misfires that trigger atrial fibrillation.

items.name: Aorta
items.description: The body's main artery, leaving the left ventricle and arching over the heart before running down the chest and abdomen. Its elastic wall smooths the pulse into steady flow.
items.funFact: Its first millimetres matter most: the coronary arteries branch off immediately, before any other organ gets blood.

items.name: Aortic arch
items.description: The curved top of the aorta. Three branches leave it to supply the right arm and head, the left side of the head, and the left arm.
facts: Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
items.funFact: Baroreceptors in the arch constantly report blood pressure to the brainstem.

items.name: Descending aorta
items.description: The long straight section running down behind the heart, through the diaphragm and into the abdomen, where it becomes the abdominal aorta.
items.funFact: It is the reference vessel for the pulse wave speed used to estimate arterial stiffness.

items.name: Left main coronary artery
items.description: A short trunk from the left aortic sinus that divides into the LAD and circumflex arteries. It supplies most of the left ventricle.
items.funFact: Because it is so short, a blockage here threatens a huge share of the heart at once.

items.name: Left anterior descending artery
items.description: Runs down the front groove between the ventricles, feeding the front wall of the left ventricle and the front two-thirds of the septum.
items.funFact: It supplies the part of the ventricle that does the most work, which is why its blockages are so dangerous.

items.name: Circumflex artery
items.description: Curves around the back of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and ventricle, supplying the side and back of the left ventricle.
items.funFact: In some people it also supplies the back of the septum, taking over the right coronary's usual job.

items.name: Right coronary artery
items.description: Leaves the right aortic sinus and circles the right side of the heart, supplying the right ventricle, the back of the septum and usually the SA and AV nodes.
items.funFact: A blockage here often slows the heart as well as starving it, because it feeds the wiring.

items.name: Posterior descending artery
items.description: Runs down the back groove between the ventricles to supply the inferior wall and the back third of the septum.
items.funFact: Which artery gives rise to it defines the heart's dominance, a detail surgeons care about.

items.name: Coronary sinus
items.description: A wide venous channel on the back of the heart collecting blood from most of the heart muscle and emptying into the right atrium.
items.funFact: It carries roughly the whole coronary venous return, a few percent of cardiac output.

items.name: Cardiac veins
items.description: The great, middle and small cardiac veins running on the heart surface, draining deoxygenated muscle blood into the coronary sinus.
items.funFact: They run in the same grooves as the arteries, which is why a heart's surface looks striped.

items.name: Sinoatrial node
items.description: The heart's natural pacemaker, a small patch of specialised cells high in the right atrium. It fires spontaneously and sets the resting rhythm.
facts: Junction of SVC and right atrium
items.funFact: It is a few millimetres long and generates the electrical signal for every normal beat.

items.name: Atrioventricular node
items.description: The only electrical gateway between atria and ventricles. It delays the signal by about a tenth of a second so the atria can empty first.
items.funFact: That delay is why the P wave and the QRS complex are separated on an ECG.

items.name: Bundle of His
items.description: A short bundle of conducting fibres that carries the signal from the AV node into the ventricular septum.
items.funFact: It is the only normal wire crossing the electrical wall between atria and ventricles.

items.name: Bundle branches
items.description: Two fast-conducting branches running down each side of the septum, delivering the signal towards the ventricular apex.
items.funFact: Blocking one turns the ECG into a wide, notched shape as the ventricles activate one after the other.

items.name: Purkinje fibres
items.description: A network spreading through the ventricular walls that triggers muscle contraction almost simultaneously from the inside out.
items.funFact: They fire the inner wall a fraction before the outer wall, so the chamber squeezes inward efficiently.

items.name: Systemic circulation
items.description: The loop from the left ventricle through the aorta, arteries, arterioles, capillaries and veins back to the right atrium. It delivers oxygen and picks up waste.
items.funFact: Most of the pressure drop happens in the tiny arterioles, which is how the body redirects flow.

items.name: Pulmonary circulation
items.description: The loop from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium. Low pressure, high flow, and the place where blood picks up oxygen.
items.funFact: It handles the same volume as the systemic loop at about a fifth of the pressure.

items.name: Capillaries
items.description: Microscopic vessels one cell thick where oxygen, nutrients and drugs cross into tissue and waste crosses back.
items.funFact: Red cells deform to squeeze through: some capillaries are narrower than the cells themselves.

items.name: Artery wall
items.description: Three layers: an inner endothelium, a thick muscular and elastic middle layer that withstands pressure, and an outer supportive coat.
items.funFact: The elastic middle layer is what converts the heart's bursts into the smooth flow felt at your wrist.

items.name: Arterioles
items.description: The small resistance vessels that control how much blood each tissue receives by narrowing or widening their smooth muscle.
items.funFact: A few percent change in their diameter can shift blood pressure measurably.

items.name: Endothelium
items.description: A single layer of flat cells lining every vessel and the heart's interior. It senses flow, controls clotting and releases nitric oxide to relax the vessel.
items.funFact: It is the body's largest organ by surface area if you unfold all the vessels.

items.name: Venous valves
items.description: Pocket-like flaps inside veins that allow flow only towards the heart, so blood is not dragged backwards by gravity.
items.funFact: Calf muscles act as a second pump, squeezing veins that valves then keep emptied.

items.name: Cardiomyocyte
items.description: A branched, striated muscle cell packed with mitochondria and coupled to its neighbours so the whole wall contracts as one unit.
facts: About a third of cell volume
items.funFact: It cannot divide meaningfully after birth, so lost muscle is replaced by scar, not new pump.

items.name: Sarcomere
items.description: The repeating contractile unit inside the cell where actin and myosin filaments slide past each other to shorten the fibre.
items.funFact: Every contraction in your body is the same trick: filaments sliding, not shrinking.

items.name: Calcium trigger
items.description: Calcium entering during the action potential makes the cell release far more calcium from its internal store, which lets myosin bind actin and generate force.
items.funFact: It is calcium-induced calcium release: a small spark ignites a much bigger one.

items.name: Intercalated discs
items.description: Junctions at the ends of cardiomyocytes that mechanically grip neighbours and electrically couple them through gap junctions.
items.funFact: Gap junctions let a signal pass cell to cell so fast that the wall behaves like one giant cell.

items.name: T-tubules
items.description: Deep tube-like invaginations of the cell membrane that carry the electrical signal quickly into the centre of the cell.
items.funFact: They exist because a muscle cell is too fat for a surface signal to reach its middle in time.

items.name: Blood
items.description: The transport fluid: red cells carrying oxygen, plasma carrying dissolved substances including drugs, plus platelets and immune cells.
items.funFact: Blood is about half cells by volume, which is why it is thicker than water.
